title: Geometry and measurement across cultures and careers
learning_goals: Investigate a geometric idea or measurement practice using a specific, cited cultural or community source.
Describe mathematical features such as circles, polygons, symmetry, repetition, scale, or measurement without reducing cultural meaning to mathematics alone.
Connect geometric and measurement reasoning to careers or disciplines while separating sourced facts from our own mathematical analysis.
success_criteria: I name the source, place or community, object or practice, and the geometric feature I am analysing.
I distinguish what the cultural source actually says from a mathematical observation I make from a diagram or construction.
I explain one responsible career or interdisciplinary connection and identify a question that still needs cultural or expert review.

vocabulary.meaning: a reproducible process for creating points, lines, circles, angles, or polygons from stated constraints
a transformation or balanced arrangement that leaves selected geometric relationships unchanged
a repeated visual element that may carry artistic, cultural, structural, or symbolic meaning in a larger design
the historical, social, religious, artistic, or community setting needed to interpret a practice responsibly
identifying where information or an image came from so a reader can check its meaning and limits

why_it_matters: Geometry is used in art, architecture, design, surveying, navigation, manufacturing, and many community practices. Studying a sourced example can reveal powerful mathematical structure, but responsible analysis also requires us to avoid treating an entire culture as a pattern library or assuming that our geometric description explains the work's full meaning.

direct_instruction.heading: Begin with the cultural source, not the pattern alone
direct_instruction.body: Use a museum, community, educational, or scholarly source that names the object or practice and gives enough context to avoid guessing at its meaning. Record the source and what it explicitly states. A mathematical observation such as 'I can trace an eight-point star from overlapping squares' is our analysis unless the source itself makes that claim.

direct_instruction.heading: Describe structure with reproducible geometry
direct_instruction.body: Choose a bounded feature to investigate: circles and polygons, repeated angles, symmetry, tessellation, scale, or a measurement system. Mark centres, radii, parallel lines, repeated units, or transformations on a separate study diagram rather than altering the cultural image. Explain a construction or measurement procedure another learner can repeat.

direct_instruction.heading: Connect without flattening context
direct_instruction.body: Link the geometric reasoning to a field such as architecture, carpentry, graphic design, conservation, engineering, machining, surveying, or digital modelling. State what mathematics transfers to the career and what does not. Keep religious, historical, and cultural interpretations attached to appropriate sources and leave unresolved cultural claims for educator or community review.

method_routes.title: Artifact-and-evidence case-study route
steps: Choose one specifically sourced object, building detail, map, tool, or design practice.
Record the source's cultural and historical description before adding mathematical labels.
Create a separate geometric study diagram showing only defensible shapes, relationships, or measurements.
Reconstruct or calculate one feature with a ruler, compass, grid, or coordinate method.
Write a mathematics finding, a cultural-context statement, and a question that remains outside the mathematical evidence.
method_routes.when_useful: Use this route when a museum, community, or scholarly source provides a concrete artifact or design that can be studied without inventing its meaning.
method_routes.check: Every cultural statement must be source-attributed, while every new geometric claim must be reproducible from the cited image, dimensions, or construction.

method_routes.title: Compare measurement systems in use
steps: Identify two measurement systems or conventions used in a documented context.
Name the quantities and units being measured and whether conversions are exact or approximate.
Measure or convert the same physical quantity under each system using stated factors.
Compare convenience, precision, error risks, tools, and career context rather than declaring one culture mathematically superior.
State which conclusion follows from measurement evidence and which historical question needs another source.
method_routes.when_useful: Use this route when a trade, science, historical, or community practice uses a measurement convention that can be compared quantitatively with SI or another documented system.
method_routes.check: The comparison must preserve units and conversion assumptions and must not turn a technical difference into a ranking of peoples or cultures.

representations.label: Annotated geometric study diagram
representations.description: A separate diagram traces selected circles, polygons, axes, angles, or repeated units and labels which features are source facts versus learner analysis.
representations.text_alternative: State the source object and context, then list each traced geometric feature, its measurements or construction, evidence status, and any cultural interpretation left to the source.

representations.label: Context-mathematics-career map
representations.description: A three-part map separates sourced cultural context, mathematical analysis, and one career or disciplinary application so that none is presented as a substitute for another.
representations.text_alternative: Read the source context first, then the geometric relationship investigated, then the transferable career skill, followed by limits and unanswered review questions.

worked_examples.prompt: Use the Metropolitan Museum educator resource to analyse a ruler-and-compass star construction without claiming that the geometry explains all meaning in Islamic art.

steps.label: Source the context
steps.explanation: Record that the museum resource presents geometric design in works from the Islamic world and includes classroom pattern-making activities; do not generalize one design to every region or period.

steps.label: Reconstruct one feature
steps.explanation: Draw a circle, mark four perpendicular diameters, connect alternating points to form two overlapping squares, and note the eight equally spaced directions created by the construction.

steps.label: Bound the interpretation
steps.explanation: Describe the repeated angles, symmetry, and construction as mathematical observations, while leaving religious, artistic, and historical meaning attached to museum or specialist sources.

worked_examples.answer: The study can responsibly report that this reconstructed design uses circles, rotated squares, repeated angles, and rotational structure; it cannot conclude that those features carry one universal meaning across Islamic art.
worked_examples.verification: The answer separates museum-supported context from a reproducible geometric construction and explicitly rejects a culture-wide interpretation.

worked_examples.prompt: A fabrication drawing gives a length as 12.0 in and a partner shop works in millimetres. Compare the measurement conventions for production communication.

steps.label: Use an exact factor
steps.explanation: Use 1 inch = 25.4 millimetres exactly, so 12.0 in corresponds numerically to 304.8 mm.

steps.label: Preserve precision
steps.explanation: The written 12.0 in may communicate different measurement precision than 304.8000 mm; conversion does not create new physical accuracy.

steps.label: Connect to practice
steps.explanation: A drawing should state the governing unit system and tolerances so fabrication, inspection, and procurement do not silently mix conventions.

worked_examples.answer: 12.0 in converts to 304.8 mm using the exact inch definition, but the production document must also preserve the intended tolerance and measurement precision.
worked_examples.verification: The arithmetic conversion is exact while the explanation correctly distinguishes unit definition from manufacturing tolerance and measured accuracy.

misconceptions.claim: If I can see symmetry, I understand what a cultural design means.
misconceptions.correction: Symmetry is a mathematical feature; cultural, religious, artistic, and historical meaning requires appropriate sources and cannot be inferred from geometry alone.

misconceptions.claim: A measurement conversion changes the physical object.
misconceptions.correction: A valid conversion expresses the same quantity in another unit; only rounding, tolerance, or measurement error can change the represented precision.

misconceptions.claim: A design seen in one museum object represents an entire culture.
misconceptions.correction: A specific object supports claims about that sourced object and context, not universal claims about all people, places, or periods.

guided.prompt: Which statement is a mathematical observation rather than a cultural interpretation?

options: The traced design has four reflection axes.
The pattern has one universal spiritual meaning.
Everyone from the region used the same design.
The object proves one culture valued geometry more.
response.correct_answer: The traced design has four reflection axes.

guided.rationale: Axes can be checked from the diagram; the other statements require cultural evidence or make unsupported generalizations.

guided.prompt: Convert 5 inches to millimetres using 1 in = 25.4 mm.
Explain how to analyse geometry in a culturally specific object without claiming that mathematics explains its full meaning.

criteria: names a credible source and specific object or practice
separates source statements from learner geometric observations
states a limit or review question
response.sample_response: I would cite the museum or community source for the object's name, place, period, and stated meaning. On a separate diagram I would trace only geometric features I can justify, such as circles or symmetry. I would label those as my mathematical analysis and leave cultural interpretation to the source and further review.

guided.rationale: Responsible mathematical study keeps cultural evidence and geometric inference distinguishable.

independent.prompt: Which source is strongest for a claim about the history of a specific museum object?

options: the museum's catalog or curator material for that object
response.correct_answer: the museum's catalog or curator material for that object

independent.rationale: Object-specific curatorial material gives traceable provenance and context that a geometric calculation cannot supply.

independent.prompt: Which career most directly uses geometric tolerances and unit-controlled drawings?
independent.rationale: Manufacturing drawings use geometry, dimensions, units, and tolerances to communicate parts and inspection requirements.

independent.prompt: A drawing shows 250 mm. Express this length in metres.
independent.rationale: One metre is 1000 millimetres, so divide 250 by 1000.

independent.prompt: Which statement best preserves source boundaries?

options: The museum identifies the object; I identify two lines that appear parallel in my study diagram.
This one object proves all related cultures used identical geometry.
My compass construction proves the artifact's religious meaning.
A conversion factor proves why a historical community chose its units.
response.correct_answer: The museum identifies the object; I identify two lines that appear parallel in my study diagram.

independent.rationale: The statement separates a sourced identification from a limited learner observation.

independent.prompt: Design a short evidence card for a geometry-and-culture case study.

criteria: identifies a specific source and context
response.sample_response: Source: a named museum educator page about one geometric panel. Context: identify the place, period, and object exactly as the source does. Mathematics: reconstruct one repeated polygon with compass and straightedge and measure its angles. Career link: conservation or architectural documentation. Limit: do not infer symbolism or community meaning beyond the cited source.

independent.rationale: An evidence card keeps the investigation auditable and prevents geometric analysis from replacing cultural context.

retrieval.prompt: What word describes identifying where information or an image came from?
retrieval.rationale: Source attribution lets another reader trace and evaluate the evidence.

retrieval.prompt: What stays the same when a length is correctly converted from centimetres to millimetres?
retrieval.rationale: Only the numerical representation and unit change; the underlying length remains the same.

retrieval.prompt: Why should a cultural geometry lesson keep a human cultural-review gate even when all calculations are correct?

criteria: distinguishes mathematical correctness from contextual accuracy
mentions risk of stereotyping or unsupported meaning
identifies value of source or community expertise
response.sample_response: Correct measurements can still sit beside a misleading cultural claim. Human review can check language, context, attribution, and whether an example stereotypes or assigns unsupported meaning, while the mathematical verifier checks the geometry and item structure.

retrieval.rationale: Cultural responsibility includes interpretation and representation questions that arithmetic tests cannot settle.

reflection_prompt: Which part of your case study is a source fact, which part is your mathematical analysis, and what would you ask a cultural or subject-matter reviewer before publication?

accessibility.nonvisual_route: Every image-based case study is paired with a linear description naming the source object, context, geometric features, measurements, construction steps, evidence labels, and interpretation limits.
response_options: spoken geometric reconstruction with cited notes
